attackPlan.title: The 4-Step Attack Plan
attackPlan.description: Follow this rigid process for EVERY True/False/Not Given question. Memorize it.

steps.title: ANALYZE the Statement
steps.description: Underline the KEY CLAIM. Circle qualifiers like 'some,' 'all,' 'most,' 'never,' 'always.' Note numbers, dates, names.
steps.example: Statement: 'Most farmers now use organic methods.' → Key claim: MOST farmers, ORGANIC methods.

steps.title: LOCATE the Paragraph
steps.description: Scan for keywords or synonyms. Statements usually follow passage order. Find the 1-3 sentences discussing this topic.

steps.title: COMPARE Meaning (Not Words)
steps.description: Read the passage section carefully. Does it SAY THE SAME THING (TRUE), SAY THE OPPOSITE (FALSE), or NOT MENTION IT (NOT GIVEN)?
steps.example: Passage: 'the majority still rely heavily on chemical pesticides' → OPPOSITE of 'most use organic' → FALSE.

steps.title: ELIMINATE Doubt
steps.description: For TRUE/FALSE: Can you quote the evidence? For NOT GIVEN: Are you 100% sure it's not mentioned anywhere? If unsure between FALSE and NOT GIVEN, it's usually NOT GIVEN.
steps.proTip: NOT GIVEN is the most common answer when you're uncertain. The passage will CLEARLY confirm or contradict TRUE/FALSE answers.

howTheyTrickYou.title: How They Will Trick You (Distractor Patterns)
howTheyTrickYou.description: IELTS examiners use specific traps. Learn to spot them.

traps.name: The 'Sounds Logical' Trap
traps.theTrick: The statement seems true based on common sense, but the passage never mentions it.

example.passage: Urban beekeeping programs could help stabilize bee populations in cities.
example.statement: Urban beekeeping is cheaper than rural beekeeping.
example.wrongThinking: This seems logical—cities have less space, so it must be cheaper.
example.defense: The passage NEVER compares costs. Don't use logic—only use what's written.

traps.name: The 'Almost the Same Number' Trap
traps.theTrick: The passage says '30%' but the statement says 'one-third' (33%). Close, but not exact.

example.passage: 30% of students reported connectivity issues.
example.statement: One-third of students experience technical problems.
example.wrongThinking: 30% is close to 33%, so it's TRUE.
example.defense: 30% ≠ one-third (33.3%). IELTS tests precision. If the numbers don't match exactly, it's FALSE.

traps.name: The 'Qualifier Swap' Trap
traps.theTrick: The passage uses 'some' or 'most,' but the statement uses 'all' or 'never.'

example.passage: Most farmers still rely heavily on chemical pesticides.
example.statement: All farmers use chemical pesticides.
example.wrongThinking: Most means almost all, so it's basically TRUE.
example.defense: 'Most' ≠ 'All.' Even one farmer using organic methods makes 'all' FALSE.

traps.name: The 'Partial Information' Trap
traps.theTrick: The passage mentions PART of the statement but not the full claim.

example.passage: Professor Chen is from Melbourne University.
example.statement: Professor Chen's research was conducted at Melbourne University.
example.wrongThinking: She's from Melbourne, so her research must be there too.
example.defense: The passage says WHERE SHE WORKS, not WHERE THE RESEARCH HAPPENED. Missing info = NOT GIVEN.

traps.name: The 'Extreme Language' Trap
traps.theTrick: The statement uses absolute words ('always,' 'never,' 'completely') when the passage uses qualified language ('could,' 'might,' 'often').

example.passage: Urban beekeeping could help stabilize bee populations.
example.statement: Urban beekeeping can completely solve the bee crisis.
example.wrongThinking: 'Help stabilize' means it solves the problem.
example.correctAnswer: NOT GIVEN (or FALSE if passage says it's partial)
example.defense: 'Could help' ≠ 'completely solve.' Watch for extreme claims.

seeItInAction.title: See It in Action (Mini-Example)
seeItInAction.description: Here's how to apply the 4-Step Attack Plan to a real question.
seeItInAction.theText: The honey bee population has declined by 30% over the past decade due to pesticide use and habitat loss. Scientists at Cambridge University have been studying this phenomenon since 2018. While some farmers have switched to organic methods, the majority still rely heavily on chemical pesticides.
seeItInAction.theQuestion: Most farmers now use organic farming methods.

theSolution.step1: ANALYZE: Key claim = 'MOST farmers' + 'USE organic methods' (present tense).
theSolution.step2: LOCATE: Scan for 'farmers,' 'organic,' 'chemical.' Found in sentence 3.
theSolution.step3: COMPARE: Passage says 'the majority still rely heavily on chemical pesticides.' This is the OPPOSITE of 'most use organic.'
theSolution.step4: ELIMINATE: Can I quote evidence? YES: 'the majority still rely heavily on chemical pesticides.' This CONTRADICTS the statement.
theSolution.whyNotTrue: 'Some farmers have switched' ≠ 'most farmers.' The passage explicitly says the MAJORITY use chemicals.
theSolution.whyNotNotGiven: The passage DIRECTLY addresses what most farmers do. It's not missing information—it's a clear contradiction.

tips.explanation: Question 1's answer is near the start, Question 5's is near the end. Use this to locate information faster.

tips.tip: NOT GIVEN is your friend when uncertain
tips.explanation: If you can't find clear evidence for TRUE or FALSE after 60 seconds, choose NOT GIVEN. TRUE/FALSE answers are ALWAYS clearly supported or contradicted.
IELTS never uses the exact same words. 'Declined by 30%' = 'fallen by 30%' = 'decreased by 30%.' Train your brain to spot paraphrases.
The second you see 'all,' 'most,' 'some,' 'never,' 'always,' circle it. These words are where 90% of traps hide.

trapPatterns.description: Watch for misleading statements and distractors.
examples: Statements that are true in real life but not mentioned in the passage
Numbers or facts that are almost—but not exactly—the same
Information appearing in a different context
Extreme language (always, never, all) when passage uses qualified language
trapPatterns.warningSigns: Absolute terms like 'always,' 'never,' or 'all' often indicate FALSE answers when the passage uses more nuanced language.

difficultyPatterns: Earlier questions usually follow passage order; later ones may not
If you find info for one statement, nearby questions might be related
advancedTips.confidenceBooster: Information for TRUE and FALSE answers will always be clearly stated or clearly contradicted. If you're unsure, it's likely NOT GIVEN.

timeManagement.priority: Do AFTER gap-fill/sentence completion (those are faster)
timeManagement.tip: If stuck for 90+ seconds, guess NOT GIVEN and move on. You can't afford to spend 3 minutes on one question.

subsections.title: 1.1 Overview
subsections.content: True/False/Not Given (T/F/NG) is one of the most common and challenging question types in the IELTS Academic and General Training Reading tests. You are given a series of statements and must decide whether each one agrees with, contradicts, or is not mentioned in the passage.

answerMeanings.meaning: The statement agrees with the information in the passage
The statement contradicts the information in the passage
There is no information about this in the passage

importantNote.title: Important Note
importantNote.description: In some IELTS tests, you'll see 'Yes/No/Not Given' instead. The difference:
importantNote.note: The strategy for both is essentially the same.

subsections.title: 1.2 What This Question Type Tests
subsections.description: T/F/NG questions assess several critical reading skills:

skills.meaning: Understanding specific information, not just general ideas
Recognizing when the same meaning is expressed differently
Knowing what the text actually says vs. what you assume
Paying attention to qualifiers, negatives, and scope
Matching claims against textual evidence

subsections.keyInsight: This question type does NOT test your opinion or general knowledge. It ONLY tests whether information appears in the passage and whether the statement matches it.

subsections.title: 2.1 TRUE вЂ” The Statement Agrees
subsections.description: The answer is TRUE when:
criteria: The passage explicitly states the same information (possibly using different words)
The statement is a valid paraphrase of passage content
You can point to specific text that confirms the statement

example.passage: The research team discovered that dolphins can recognize themselves in mirrors, a capability previously thought to exist only in great apes and humans.
example.statement: Before this research, scientists believed only great apes and humans could identify their own reflection.
example.explanation: The statement paraphrases 'capability previously thought to exist only in great apes and humans.' The meaning is identical.

subsections.title: 2.2 FALSE вЂ” The Statement Contradicts
subsections.description: The answer is FALSE when:
criteria: The passage states the OPPOSITE of what the statement claims
There is a direct, demonstrable contradiction
You can quote text that conflicts with the statement
subsections.criticalPoint: FALSE requires contradiction, not just absence. The passage must say something incompatible with the statement.

example.passage: The survey revealed that 68% of respondents preferred working from home at least three days per week.
example.statement: The majority of people surveyed wanted to work in the office most of the week.
example.explanation: 68% preferred working from home at least three days directly contradicts 'wanted to work in the office most of the week.' These cannot both be true.

subsections.title: 2.3 NOT GIVEN вЂ” No Information
subsections.description: The answer is NOT GIVEN when:
criteria: The passage does not mention this specific information at all
The topic might be related, but the specific claim is never addressed
You cannot find evidence to confirm OR deny the statement
subsections.criticalPoint: NOT GIVEN means absence of information. You cannot infer, assume, or use logic to determine the answerвЂ”the passage simply doesn't discuss it.

example.passage: The research team discovered that dolphins can recognize themselves in mirrors. The study was conducted at a marine facility in California over a period of two years.
example.statement: The research was funded by the US government.
example.explanation: The passage mentions where and how long the study took place, but says nothing about funding. We cannot assume anything about funding sources.

commonPitfalls.title: Common Mistakes & Pitfalls
commonPitfalls.description: The 10 Most Common Errors Students Make

mistakes.title: Using Outside Knowledge
mistakes.trap: You know something is true in real life, so you mark it TRUE.

example.passage: Passage discusses climate change but doesn't mention CO2.
example.statement: Carbon dioxide is a greenhouse gas.
example.wrongThinking: I know CO2 is a greenhouse gas, so TRUE.
example.correctThinking: The passage doesn't mention CO2 at all в†’ NOT GIVEN

mistakes.rule: Only use information IN the passage. Your knowledge is irrelevant.

mistakes.title: Confusing FALSE and NOT GIVEN
mistakes.trap: The statement seems wrong, so you choose FALSEвЂ”but the passage never discusses it.

example.passage: The experiment used 50 participants over three months.
example.statement: The experiment was expensive to conduct.
example.wrongThinking: 50 participants sounds expensive, but the passage doesn't say it was expensive, so FALSE.
example.correctThinking: Cost is never mentioned в†’ NOT GIVEN

mistakes.rule: FALSE needs a contradiction. No information = NOT GIVEN.

mistakes.title: Over-Inferencing for TRUE
mistakes.trap: You make a logical assumption and treat it as confirmed.

example.passage: The CEO announced the company would expand into Asian markets.
example.statement: The company expects expansion to be profitable.
example.wrongThinking: Why would they expand if not for profit? TRUE.
example.correctThinking: Profitability expectations are never stated в†’ NOT GIVEN

mistakes.rule: TRUE requires explicit support, not logical assumptions.

mistakes.title: Missing Paraphrases
mistakes.trap: You don't recognize that the passage says the same thing differently.

example.passage: The population declined rapidly.
example.statement: The number of inhabitants fell quickly.
example.wrongThinking: I can't find the words 'inhabitants' or 'fell' в†’ NOT GIVEN.
example.correctThinking: 'population' = 'number of inhabitants'; 'declined rapidly' = 'fell quickly' в†’ TRUE

mistakes.rule: Learn to recognize synonyms and paraphrases.

mistakes.title: Ignoring Qualifiers
mistakes.trap: You miss small words that change meaning significantly.

mistakes.title: Reversing Comparisons
mistakes.trap: You confuse which item is greater/lesser/earlier/later.

example.passage: Method A was more effective than Method B.
example.statement: Method B produced better results than Method A.
example.wrongThinking: It's comparing the two methods, so TRUE.
example.correctThinking: The passage says A > B, but statement says B > A в†’ FALSE

mistakes.title: Scope Errors
mistakes.trap: The statement makes a broader or narrower claim than the passage.

example.passage: The study found that children who read daily performed better in school.
example.statement: Reading daily improves academic performance for all age groups.
example.correctThinking: Passage is about children only; statement claims ALL age groups в†’ NOT GIVEN

mistakes.title: Partial Matches
mistakes.trap: Part of the statement is true, but another part is false or unconfirmed.

example.passage: Dr. Smith, a biologist from Oxford, published the findings in 2020.
example.statement: Dr. Smith, a chemist from Oxford, published the findings in 2020.
example.reasoning: One contradiction makes the whole statement false

mistakes.rule: Every part of the statement must be verified. One wrong element = FALSE.

mistakes.title: Misreading Negatives
mistakes.trap: Double negatives or negative constructions confuse you.

mistakes.title: Position Assumption
mistakes.trap: You assume statements at the end of the question set relate to the end of the passage.
mistakes.reality: While questions generally follow passage order, this isn't guaranteed. Always verify the location.
mistakes.strategy: Use keywords to locate the relevant section, don't rely on position alone.

questionTypes.name: Matching Headings
questionTypes.frequency: High - appears in approximately 60-70% of IELTS Reading tests

howToIdentify: A list of headings (usually labeled i, ii, iii, iv, etc.)
Instructions say 'Choose the correct heading for each paragraph/section'
More headings than paragraphs (distractors included)

examples.passage:
Paragraph A: The company's revenue increased by 20% last year. This growth was driven by a successful marketing campaign in Asia.
Paragraph B: Employee turnover remains a challenge, with high rates of resignation in the customer support department.

questions.text: Heading for Paragraph A
questions.explanation: Paragraph A discusses revenue increase (financial success) and Asia (regional growth).

subsections.title: 1.1 Overview
subsections.content: In this task, you are given a list of headings (marked with Roman numerals: i, ii, iii, iv...) and a text divided into sections or paragraphs (marked A, B, C...). Your task is to choose the heading that best reflects the main idea of each paragraph. There will always be more headings than paragraphs. This means some headings are 'distractors' that you will not use.

subsections.title: 1.2 What This Question Type Tests
subsections.description: Matching Headings assesses your ability to distinguish the 'Gist' (the overall meaning) from specific details.

skills.meaning: Reading quickly to understand the general theme
Finding the core message of a block of text
Telling the difference between a main point and a supporting example
Recognizing that the heading summarizes the text using different words

subsections.keyInsight: This is arguably the most difficult reading task because you cannot simply look for keywords. You must understand the purpose of the paragraph.

subsections.title: 2.1 The Role of a Heading
subsections.content: A correct heading acts like a Title. It must cover the content of the entire paragraph, not just one sentence within it.

example.heading: The financial cost of space travel
example.requirement: The Paragraph must discuss money, budget, or expenses throughout the majority of the text

subsections.title: 2.2 The Role of Distractors
subsections.content: The extra headings are not random. They are designed to trick you.
criteria: The Detail Distractor: A heading that covers only one specific sentence or example in the paragraph, but not the main idea
The Keyword Distractor: A heading that contains a specific word found in the text, but the meaning does not match

sections.title: SECTION 3: THE KEY DISTINCTION вЂ” MAIN IDEA vs. SUPPORTING DETAIL
sections.intro: This is where most students lose marks. You must learn to ignore details when looking for the main idea.

Main Idea: The writer's primary argument or topic
Supporting Detail: Statistics, names, dates, or examples used to prove the main idea

subsections.title: 3.2 The Scope Test
subsections.content: When you think you have found the right heading, ask yourself: 'Does this heading cover 80% of the paragraph, or only 20%?'

subsections.title: 3.3 Comparison Example
subsections.passage: While solar power is becoming cheaper, the initial installation cost remains a barrier for many households. Homeowners must pay thousands of dollars upfront for panels and batteries. Although government subsidies exist, they often do not cover the full expense, making solar energy a luxury for the wealthy.

examples.heading: The declining price of technology
examples.analysis: Detail - mentioned in the first clause only

examples.heading: Financial obstacles to adopting solar power
examples.analysis: Main Idea - covers the whole paragraph

steps.title: Analyze the Headings First
actions: Read the list of headings before the text
Try to identify the difference between similar headings

steps.title: Read Paragraph A (Topic Sentences)
actions: Read the first two sentences and the last sentence of the paragraph
The main idea is often located here
Warning: If the paragraph starts with a story or example, the main idea is likely in the middle

steps.title: Create Your Own Title
actions: Before looking back at the list, ask yourself: 'In three words, what was this paragraph about?'

steps.title: Match and Eliminate
actions: Look for the heading that matches your summary
If you find a match, write it down and cross it off the list
If unsure between two headings, write both (e.g., A = iv / vi) and move on

subsections.title: 4.2 Signal Words to Watch
subsections.content: Writers use specific words to signal the main idea.

categories.rule: The main idea is usually after these words
categories.example: Many people think X. However, the reality is Y. в†’ The main idea is Y

categories.category: Conclusion Words (Therefore, Thus, As a result)
categories.rule: These usually summarize the main point

subsections.title: Passage Excerpt
subsections.passage: For centuries, the construction of bridges involved locally sourced materials such as wood and stone. These materials were abundant and cheap, but they limited the span and durability of the structures. Wooden bridges would rot, and stone bridges were difficult to build over deep water. It wasn't until the Industrial Revolution brought iron and steel that engineers could span great distances.
headings: i. The environmental impact of bridges
ii. Why modern bridges are superior
iii. Limitations of early building materials
subsections.question: Which heading matches Paragraph A?

examples.heading: i. Environmental impact
examples.analysis: NOT GIVEN. The text mentions materials, but not their impact on nature

examples.heading: iv. Industrial Revolution
examples.analysis: TRAP. It is mentioned in the last sentence, but it is not what the whole paragraph is about

examples.heading: ii. Modern bridges superior
examples.analysis: CLOSE. It implies modern materials are better, but the focus is on the past

examples.heading: iii. Limitations of early materials
examples.analysis: CORRECT. The paragraph lists wood and stone (early materials) and explains why they were bad (limited span, rot, hard to build)

commonPitfalls.title: Common Mistakes & Pitfalls
commonPitfalls.description: The 8 Most Common Errors Students Make

mistakes.title: Matching Keywords (The 'Word Spot' Trap)
mistakes.trap: You see the word 'Volcano' in the text and 'Volcanic' in the heading, so you match them immediately.
mistakes.rule: Read the sentence containing the word. Does the heading describe the whole paragraph or just that one word? Usually, exact word matches are traps.

mistakes.title: Reading Only the First Sentence
mistakes.trap: You rely 100% on the first sentence.
mistakes.rule: While often true, the main idea can be in the second sentence (especially if the first sentence is a 'hook' or a rhetorical question). Always check the middle and end.

mistakes.title: Spending Too Much Time on One Paragraph
mistakes.trap: You spend 5 minutes staring at Paragraph B because you can't decide.
mistakes.rule: If you are stuck, leave it. Do the easier paragraphs first. When you come back, you will have fewer headings to choose from.

mistakes.title: Not Crossing Out Used Headings
mistakes.trap: You keep re-reading the full list of headings for every single paragraph.
mistakes.rule: Eliminate headings as you go. This saves mental energy and reduces confusion.

mistakes.title: Confusing Examples with Main Points
mistakes.trap: The paragraph tells a story about a specific farmer. You choose a heading about 'Farming methods.'
mistakes.rule: The farmer is just an example. What point is the writer proving by using the farmer?

mistakes.title: Ignoring Distractors
mistakes.trap: You forget that there are 2-3 extra headings that you will not use.
mistakes.rule: Do not force a heading to fit just because it's left over. It might be a distractor.

mistakes.title: Looking for Specific Details
mistakes.trap: You treat this like a 'Gap Fill' question, looking for names and dates.
mistakes.rule: Switch your brain to 'Summary Mode.' You are looking for general themes, not specific data points.

mistakes.title: Ignoring Plurals
mistakes.trap: The heading says 'The causes of poverty' (Plural). The paragraph discusses only one cause.
mistakes.rule: If the heading is plural, the paragraph must list more than one factor. If it only lists one, that heading is wrong.

questionTypes.name: Multiple Choice
questionTypes.frequency: High - appears in almost every IELTS Reading test

howToIdentify: A question or incomplete sentence followed by 3-4 options (A, B, C, D)
Instruction like 'Choose the correct letter, A, B, C or D'
Sometimes asks you to choose multiple options (e.g., 'Choose TWO letters AвЂ“E')

examples.passage: IELTS reading passages are often academic in nature, covering topics from science to history. Multiple choice questions test your ability to distinguish between main ideas and supporting details.

questions.text: What type of topics do IELTS reading passages cover?
options: B) A variety of academic subjects
questions.explanation: The passage says they cover topics 'from science to history', which matches 'a variety of academic subjects'.

subsections.title: 1.1 Overview
subsections.content: Multiple Choice questions are one of the most common question types in IELTS Reading. You are given a question or incomplete sentence, followed by three or four options (A, B, C, or D). Your task is to choose the option that best answers the question or completes the sentence based on information in the passage.

formats.description: Choose ONE correct answer from 3-4 options.
Choose TWO or THREE correct answers from a list of 5-7 options (instructions will specify how many to choose).

subsections.title: 1.2 What This Question Type Tests
subsections.description: Multiple Choice questions assess several critical reading skills:

skills.meaning: Understanding specific information and the writer's arguments
Reading between the lines to understand implied meaning
Recognizing when the same idea is expressed using different vocabulary
Distinguishing between what the writer states and what they believe
Ruling out incorrect options systematically
Understanding nuances, qualifiers, and scope

subsections.keyInsight: IELTS multiple choice is NOT like school tests. The incorrect options (distractors) are carefully designed to trap you. They often contain words from the passage but with twisted meanings.

subsections.title: 2.1 The Correct Answer
subsections.description: The correct answer will:
criteria: Accurately reflect information stated or implied in the passage
Use paraphrases or synonyms (rarely exact words from the text)
Match the scope and detail level of the passage
Be fully supported by evidence you can point to

example.passage: The experiment demonstrated that regular exercise can significantly reduce symptoms of depression in adults.
example.question: What did the experiment show?
options: B) Physical activity can substantially decrease depressive symptoms in grown-ups.
C) Only adults benefit from exercise.
D) Depression is caused by lack of exercise.
example.explanation: "Physical activity" = exercise; "substantially decrease" = significantly reduce; "depressive symptoms" = symptoms of depression; "grown-ups" = adults. This is a perfect paraphrase.

subsections.title: 2.2 The Three Types of Distractors
subsections.description: Understanding how wrong answers are constructed helps you avoid them.

types.description: Contains words directly from the passage but twists the meaning or context.

example.passage: While some scientists support the theory, others remain skeptical.

types.type: Type 2: The True But Irrelevant Distractor
types.description: The statement is true according to the passage, but it doesn't answer the specific question asked.

example.question: Why did the company expand to Asia?
example.passage: The company expanded to Asia due to growing demand. It also opened offices in Europe.
example.distractor: The company opened offices in Europe.
example.explanation: True, but doesn't answer WHY they expanded to Asia

types.description: Sounds logical or relates to the topic, but is never actually stated in the passage.

example.passage: The survey included 500 participants from major cities.
example.distractor: The survey was expensive to conduct.
example.explanation: Logical assumption, but cost is never mentioned

sections.title: SECTION 3: THE KEY DISTINCTION вЂ” STATED vs. IMPLIED vs. ASSUMED

characteristics: Not directly stated but can be logically concluded from passage evidence
Requires inference but must be based on text
The writer suggests it without saying it explicitly
Based on your own knowledge or logic
NOT in the passage at all

subsections.title: 3.2 Testing Inference
subsections.description: IELTS sometimes asks you to infer (read between the lines). This is different from assuming.

example.passage: Sales dropped by 40% after the scandal broke. The CEO resigned three months later.
example.question: What does the writer suggest about the CEO's resignation?
example.validInference: It was related to poor company performance. (Timing and context suggest connection)
example.invalidAssumption: The CEO was personally involved in the scandal. (Never stated or implied)

subsections.rule: Inference must be supported by textual evidence. If you're using outside knowledge, it's wrong.

steps.title: Read the Question Carefully
actions: Identify what it's asking: Fact? Opinion? Reason? Result?
Note key words: Why? What? How? According to the writer?
Underline important qualifiers: main reason, primary purpose, most likely

steps.title: Predict Before Looking at Options
actions: If possible, think of the answer in your own words first
This prevents distractors from influencing you
Locate the relevant section of the passage

steps.title: Locate the Relevant Section
actions: Questions usually follow passage order (Q1 в†’ early, Q5 в†’ later)
Scan for keywords or paraphrases from the question
Read 2-3 sentences around the keyword for context

steps.title: Eliminate Wrong Answers
actions: Cross out obviously wrong options first
Use the "distractor types" knowledge: Does it twist words from the passage? Is it true but doesn't answer the question? Is it never mentioned?

steps.title: Compare Remaining Options
actions: Read the passage section again carefully
Check every word in the remaining options against the text
Choose the option that matches most accurately

steps.title: Verify Your Answer
actions: Can you point to specific text that supports your choice?
Does your answer actually respond to the question asked?
Have you avoided choosing based on outside knowledge?

subsections.title: 4.2 Time Management
subsections.warning: Multiple choice questions can be time-consuming because you must read each option carefully. Don't spend more than 1.5 minutes per question.

examples: The main purpose of paragraph 3 is to...
The writer mentions X in order to...
categories.lookFor: Phrases like "to illustrate," "for example," "this shows that"

examples: What does the writer suggest about...?
The writer's attitude towards X is...
categories.lookFor: Opinion verbs (argue, claim, believe), evaluative adjectives (surprisingly, unfortunately)
because, due to, as a result, therefore, consequently, led to

examples: How does X differ from Y?
categories.lookFor: whereas, while, in contrast, unlike, more/less than

sections.title: SECTION 5: EXAMPLE WALKTHROUGH
sections.passage: The adoption of electric vehicles (EVs) has been slower than many environmentalists hoped. While the technology has improved dramatically over the past decade, with battery range now exceeding 300 miles for most models, the high purchase price remains a significant barrier for average consumers. Government incentives have helped in some markets, particularly in Norway, where EVs now account for over 50% of new car sales. However, in countries without such subsidies, adoption rates remain below 5%. Industry analysts believe that prices must fall by at least 30% before EVs become mainstream in these markets.

examples.question: What is identified as the main obstacle to electric vehicle adoption?
options: C) The cost of purchasing electric vehicles
D) Consumer awareness of environmental issues

explanation.A: WRONG: The passage states battery range "now exceeding 300 miles" and "technology has improved dramatically," so this is NOT presented as a current obstacle.
explanation.B: WRONG: This is a "True but Irrelevant" distractor. Government support IS mentioned, but as something that helps in some markets, not as the main obstacle overall.
explanation.C: CORRECT: "High purchase price remains a significant barrier" directly identifies cost as the main obstacle.
explanation.D: WRONG: Not mentioned. This is an assumption.

examples.question: According to the passage, what must happen for electric vehicles to become widely popular in markets without subsidies?
options: A) Battery technology must improve further
B) Prices need to decrease by approximately one-third
C) More charging stations must be built

explanation.A: WRONG: Technology has already improved; this is not presented as a requirement.
explanation.B: CORRECT: "Prices must fall by at least 30% before EVs become mainstream in these markets" (30% = approximately one-third).
explanation.C: WRONG: Charging infrastructure is never mentioned.
explanation.D: WRONG: Not mentionedвЂ”this is an assumption based on general knowledge.

examples.question: What does the writer suggest about Norway's electric vehicle market?
options: A) It has been unsuccessful despite government efforts
B) It demonstrates the effectiveness of financial incentives
C) It has the best battery technology in the world
D) It relies entirely on environmental awareness

explanation.A: WRONG: Contradicts the passageвЂ”over 50% is clearly successful.
explanation.B: CORRECT: This requires inference. The writer states "Government incentives have helped" and then gives Norway as an example where "EVs now account for over 50%." The implication is that incentives led to success.
explanation.C: WRONG: Not mentioned. Word match trapвЂ”"technology" appears in the passage but not in this context.

commonPitfalls.title: COMMON MISTAKES & PITFALLS
commonPitfalls.description: The 10 Most Common Errors Students Make

mistakes.title: Choosing the First "True" Statement
mistakes.trap: You find an option that is factually correct according to the passage, so you choose it immediately.

example.question: What was the main reason for the policy change?
example.optionB: The policy was introduced in 2015. (TRUE, but doesn't answer WHY)
example.optionC: Public health concerns prompted the revision. (TRUE and answers the question)

mistakes.correct: Always check that your answer actually responds to the specific question asked, not just that it's a true statement.

mistakes.title: Matching Words Instead of Meaning
mistakes.trap: You see the same words in the passage and in option A, so you choose it.

example.passage: The study examined various species of birds.
example.distractor: The study focused exclusively on birds.

mistakes.correct: "Various species" в‰  "exclusively." The words "study" and "birds" match, but "various" contradicts "exclusively."
mistakes.rule: IELTS expects you to recognize paraphrases. Exact word matches are often traps.

mistakes.title: Using Outside Knowledge
mistakes.trap: You know something is true in real life, so you choose it even though it's not in the passage.

example.question: According to the passage, what is a benefit of meditation?
example.distractor: It reduces blood pressure. (You know this is true, but the passage only mentions "stress reduction")

mistakes.correct: Only choose what the passage states. Your personal knowledge is irrelevant.

mistakes.title: Not Reading All Options
mistakes.trap: Option B looks good, so you select it without reading C and D.
mistakes.whyWrong: Option D might be a better, more complete answer. IELTS often has two options that are partially correct, but only one is fully accurate.
mistakes.correct: ALWAYS read all options before choosing.

mistakes.title: Ignoring Qualifiers
mistakes.trap: You miss small but critical words that change meaning.

examples.passage: Some researchers believe...

mistakes.correct: Pay attention to every word, especially qualifiers, comparatives, and absolutes.

mistakes.title: Falling for "Extreme" Language
mistakes.trap: An option uses absolute language (always, never, all, none, only, impossible) when the passage uses qualified language (often, some, many, possible).

example.passage: Renewable energy could play a significant role in reducing emissions.
example.distractor: Renewable energy will completely eliminate all emissions.

mistakes.correct: Extreme or absolute answers are usually wrong unless the passage also uses absolute language.

mistakes.title: Choosing Based on Length
mistakes.trap: You assume the longest option is correct because it has more detail, or the shortest is correct because it's simple.
mistakes.correct: Length is irrelevant. The correct answer might be the shortest or the longest. Base your choice on meaning, not appearance.

mistakes.title: Misidentifying Opinion vs. Fact
mistakes.trap: The question asks for the writer's opinion, but you choose a factual statement instead.

example.question: What is the writer's view on remote work?
example.wrong: Many companies now offer remote work. (Fact, not opinion)
example.correct: Remote work policies have been implemented too hastily. (Opinion)

mistakes.correctApproach: When asked for opinion, look for evaluative language, not just facts.

mistakes.title: Not Using Elimination
mistakes.trap: You try to find the right answer directly instead of eliminating obviously wrong options first.
mistakes.correct: It's often easier to identify what's definitely wrong than what's definitely right. Eliminate 2-3 wrong answers, then choose from the remaining options.
process: Cross out options that contradict the passage
Cross out options that are never mentioned
Cross out options that don't answer the question

mistakes.title: Overthinking Simple Questions
mistakes.trap: You spend 3 minutes analyzing a straightforward factual question, looking for hidden tricks.

example.passage: The conference will take place in Berlin.
example.question: Where will the conference be held?

mistakes.correct: Not every question is a trap. Some are straightforward. If the answer is clear and directly stated, don't second-guess yourself. Save time for harder questions.
mistakes.rule: Spend 30 seconds on simple factual questions, 1-2 minutes on inference/opinion questions.

flowchart.title: Read the Question Stem
flowchart.description: Identify what type of information you need: Fact? Opinion? Purpose? Cause/Effect?

flowchart.title: Locate the Answer Zone
flowchart.description: Find the relevant paragraph(s). Questions usually follow passage order.

flowchart.title: Read Carefully
flowchart.description: Read 2-3 sentences around the keywords. Understand the full context.

flowchart.title: Predict (if possible)
flowchart.description: Think of the answer in your own words before looking at options.

flowchart.title: Eliminate Wrong Answers
actions: True but doesn't answer the question? в†’ Eliminate

flowchart.title: Compare Remaining Options
flowchart.description: Check every word against the passage. Choose the most accurate match.

flowchart.title: Verify
flowchart.description: Can you point to evidence? Does it answer the question?

howToIdentify: Incomplete sentences with gaps
Instructions like 'NO MORE THAN THREE WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER'
Questions usually follow the order of the passage
Gaps can appear at the beginning, middle, or end of the sentence

examples.passage: The Great Barrier Reef, stretching over 2,300 kilometers along the Australian coast, is home to thousands of species of marine life. However, rising ocean temperatures have led to widespread coral bleaching, threatening the delicate ecosystem.

questions.text: The Great Barrier Reef is located along the ___________.
questions.explanation: The passage says 'along the Australian coast'. Exact extraction.

questions.text: The ecosystem is being threatened by the occurrence of ___________.
questions.explanation: The passage mentions 'widespread coral bleaching' as the threat. 'Coral bleaching' is the key phrase.

subsections.title: 1.1 Overview
subsections.content: Sentence Completion (also called Gap Fill) requires you to complete sentences using words taken directly from the passage. You are given incomplete sentences with gaps, and you must fill each gap with the exact words from the text. The instructions will specify a word limit (usually 1, 2, or 3 words, and/or a number).
typicalInstructions: Complete the sentences below. Choose NO MORE THAN THREE WORDS from the passage for each answer.
Complete the sentences using NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER from the passage.
Complete each sentence with ONE WORD ONLY from the passage.
subsections.keyInsight: This question type combines the scanning skills from Short Answer questions with the paraphrasing challenges from Matching Headings. You must find information that's expressed differently in the incomplete sentence.

subsections.title: 1.2 What This Question Type Tests
list: Scanning: Quickly locating specific information in the passage.
Paraphrase recognition: The sentence stem uses different words than the passage, but means the same thing.
Grammar awareness: Your answer must fit the grammatical structure of the sentence.
Word form recognition: Understanding whether you need a noun, verb, adjective, etc.
Precise extraction: Selecting the exact words that complete the meaning.
Following instructions: Adhering strictly to word limits.

rules.title: Rule 1: Copy Words Exactly from the Passage
rules.description: You must use the exact words as they appear.
examples: Do not change word forms (singular/plural, verb tenses)
Do not use synonyms or paraphrase
Do not add words that aren't in the passage

example.passage: The building was constructed using sustainable materials.
example.question: The construction utilized ___________.
example.correct: sustainable materials
example.wrong: eco-friendly materials (synonym, not from passage)

rules.title: Rule 2: Respect Word Limits
rules.description: Follow the same word limit rules as Short Answer questions.

example.passage: The device operates at extremely high temperatures.
example.question: The device functions at ___________.
example.correct: high temperatures (2 words)
example.wrong: extremely high temperatures (3 words - exceeds limit)

rules.title: Rule 3: Grammar Must Be Correct
rules.description: The completed sentence must be grammatically correct. Pay attention to articles, singular/plural, verb tense, and prepositions.

example.passage: ...the impact of drought conditions on plant growth.
example.question: The researchers studied the impact of ___________ on plant growth.
example.correct: drought conditions (fits: 'impact of drought conditions')
example.wrong: drought condition (grammar error - should be plural to match passage)

rules.title: Rule 4: Maintain Original Meaning
rules.description: Your completed sentence must mean the same thing as the information in the passage, even though different words are used in the sentence stem.

example.passage: Sales increased dramatically following the advertising campaign.
example.question: The advertising campaign resulted in a significant ___________ in sales.
example.correct: increase (maintains the meaning of 'increased dramatically')

types.title: Type 1: Factual Completion
types.description: These sentences test your ability to find and extract specific information (names, dates, numbers, processes, causes, etc.).

example.passage: The research was funded by the National Science Foundation.
example.question: The ___________ provided funding for the research.

types.title: Type 2: Conceptual Completion
types.description: These sentences test understanding of relationships, causes, effects, purposes, or descriptions.

example.passage: Due to rising sea levels, coastal communities face increased flooding risks.
example.question: Coastal communities are at greater risk of flooding because of ___________.

sections.title: SECTION 3: THE KEY DISTINCTION вЂ” SENTENCE STEM vs. PASSAGE WORDING

subsections.title: 3.1 Understanding Paraphrasing
subsections.content: The incomplete sentence will almost NEVER use the exact same words as the passage. This is the main challenge.

example.passage: The experiment demonstrated that regular exercise can reduce symptoms of anxiety.
example.question: The experiment showed that frequent physical activity can decrease feelings of ___________.
example.analysis: demonstrated в†’ showed; regular exercise в†’ frequent physical activity; reduce в†’ decrease; symptoms of в†’ feelings of

example.passage: Deforestation in the Amazon has accelerated over the past decade, primarily driven by agricultural expansion and illegal logging operations.
example.question: The main causes of increased deforestation in the Amazon are the growth of farming and ___________.
example.analysis: accelerated... decade в†’ increased deforestation; primarily driven by в†’ main causes; agricultural expansion в†’ growth of farming

steps.title: Read All Incomplete Sentences First
actions: Skim all sentences in the set

steps.title: Analyze the Gap
actions: Determine word type needed (noun, verb, etc.)

subsections.title: 4.2 Time Management
subsections.rationale: Takes longer than Short Answer because you must recognize paraphrases, not just scan for keywords.

beforeGap.example: 'The ___ was expensive.' в†’ need a noun
'Many ___ were studied.' в†’ need plural noun
'The device is ___' в†’ verb-ing/verb-ed or adjective

afterGap.example: '___ students attended' в†’ number or adjective

signalPatterns.pattern: The purpose of X is to ___
signalPatterns.lookFor: in order to, to, aims to
due to, because of, as a result of

subsections.title: Farming in Southeast Asia
subsections.passage: Traditional farming methods in Southeast Asia have been transformed by technological innovations over the past two decades. The introduction of automated irrigation systems has enabled farmers to reduce water consumption by up to 40% while simultaneously increasing crop yields. These systems use sensors that monitor soil moisture levels and automatically adjust water flow based on real-time conditions. However, the high initial investment requiredвЂ”typically around $15,000 per hectareвЂ”has limited adoption primarily to large-scale commercial operations. Smaller family farms continue to rely on conventional techniques due to financial constraints.

examples.question: Technological advances have changed ___________ in Southeast Asia during the last twenty years.
examples.instruction: NO MORE THAN THREE WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER
stepByStep: Read instruction: NO MORE THAN THREE WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER
Topic: Something in Southeast Asia that technology changed
Think synonyms: 'Technological advances' = 'technological innovations'; 'changed' = 'transformed'; 'last twenty years' = 'past two decades'
Scan passage: 'Traditional farming methods in Southeast Asia have been transformed by technological innovations...'
Check grammar: 'have changed traditional farming methods' вњ“

examples.question: Automated irrigation systems can decrease the amount of water used by as much as ___________.
examples.instruction: NO MORE THAN THREE WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER
stepByStep: Analyze gap: Number/percentage (indicated by 'as much as')
Think synonyms: 'decrease the amount of water used' = 'reduce water consumption'
Scan passage: 'enabled farmers to reduce water consumption by up to 40%'
Check grammar: 'by as much as 40%' вњ“

examples.question: The systems have sensors that check ___________ and control the water supply accordingly.
examples.instruction: NO MORE THAN THREE WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER
stepByStep: Think synonyms: 'check' = 'monitor'; 'control the water supply' = 'adjust water flow'
Scan passage: 'use sensors that monitor soil moisture levels...'
Check grammar: 'check soil moisture levels' вњ“

examples.question: The cost of implementing the technology is approximately ___________ for each hectare.
examples.instruction: NO MORE THAN THREE WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER
stepByStep: Think synonyms: 'cost of implementing' = 'investment required'; 'approximately' = 'typically around'
Scan passage: 'high initial investment requiredвЂ”typically around $15,000 per hectare'

examples.question: Small family farms still use traditional methods because of ___________.
examples.instruction: NO MORE THAN THREE WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER
stepByStep: Topic: Why small farms don't adopt new technology
Think synonyms: 'because of' = 'due to'; 'traditional methods' = 'conventional techniques'
Scan passage: 'Smaller family farms continue to rely on conventional techniques due to financial constraints'
Check grammar: 'because of financial constraints' вњ“

mistakes.title: Mistake 1: Ignoring Grammar Clues
mistakes.trap: You find the right topic area but choose words that don't fit grammatically.

example.passage: The research was conducted by leading scientists at Oxford University.
example.question: Oxford University's ___________ carried out the research.
example.wrong: leading scientists (redundant 'Oxford University's leading scientists')
example.correct: scientists

mistakes.rule: Read the ENTIRE sentence. Your answer must fit the grammatical structure perfectly.

mistakes.title: Mistake 2: Not Recognizing Paraphrases
mistakes.trap: You search for the exact words from the sentence stem and can't find them.

example.passage: Rising temperatures have caused polar ice to melt at unprecedented rates.
example.question: The increase in global heat has resulted in the rapid melting of ___________.
example.correct: polar ice

mistakes.rule: The sentence stem WILL use different words. Think of synonyms before scanning.

mistakes.title: Mistake 3: Exceeding Word Limits
mistakes.trap: You find a perfect phrase but it's too long.

example.passage: The device uses renewable solar energy to power operations.
example.question: The device is powered by ___________.
example.wrong: renewable solar energy (3 words)
example.correct: solar energy (2 words)

mistakes.rule: When the perfect answer is too long, keep only the essential words.

mistakes.title: Mistake 4: Changing Word Forms
mistakes.trap: You change singular to plural, or vice versa, to make it 'sound better'.

example.passage: The study examined the effect of temperature change on coral.
example.question: The research investigated how ___________ affect coral.
example.wrong: temperature changes
example.correct: temperature change

mistakes.rule: Copy words EXACTLY. Don't change forms even if you think it sounds better.

mistakes.title: Mistake 5: Including Extra Words
mistakes.trap: You include articles or prepositions that aren't needed.

example.passage: Participants were asked to complete daily exercise routines.
example.question: The participants had to do ___________ every day.
example.wrong: the daily exercise
example.correct: exercise routines (or: daily exercise)

mistakes.rule: Use minimum words. Don't add articles unless they're essential for grammar.

mistakes.title: Mistake 6: Answering from the Wrong Part of the Passage
mistakes.trap: You find a word that fits grammatically but comes from a different section.
mistakes.rule: Make sure your answer comes from the relevant section. Don't just grab a word that fits grammatically.

mistakes.title: Mistake 7: Not Reading the Full Sentence in the Passage
mistakes.trap: You find a keyword and grab the nearest noun without reading the context.

example.passage: While some countries have strict regulations, enforcement remains weak in developing nations.
example.question: In developing nations, ___________ of regulations is insufficient.
example.wrong: countries (nearby word)
example.correct: enforcement

mistakes.rule: Read the complete sentence around your keyword. Understand the full meaning.

mistakes.title: Mistake 8: Using Pronouns Instead of Nouns
mistakes.trap: The passage uses a pronoun (it, they, this) but you need the actual noun.

example.passage: Electric vehicles produce zero emissions. They also require less maintenance...
example.question: ___________ need less maintenance compared to conventional vehicles.
example.wrong: they
example.correct: Electric vehicles

mistakes.rule: If the gap requires a noun, never use a pronoun. Find what the pronoun refers to.

mistakes.title: Mistake 9: Confusing Cause and Effect
mistakes.trap: You mix up the cause with the result.

example.passage: Increased pollution has led to respiratory diseases...
example.question: Respiratory diseases are caused by ___________.
example.correct: increased pollution (the cause)

mistakes.rule: Pay attention to sentence structure. Is it asking for the cause or the effect?

mistakes.title: Mistake 10: Leaving Gaps Unfilled
mistakes.trap: You can't find the answer, so you leave it blank.
mistakes.rule: Never leave any gap empty. Use scanning + grammar clues to make your best attempt.

flowchart.title: Think of Synonyms
actions: What other words might be used?

timeManagement.tip: Gap fill takes longer than short answer due to heavy paraphrasing.

questionTypes.name: Short Answer Questions
questionTypes.frequency: Medium - appears in approximately 30-40% of IELTS Reading tests

sections.title: SECTION 1: WHAT ARE SHORT ANSWER QUESTIONS?

subsections.title: 1.1 Overview
subsections.content: Short Answer Questions require you to answer questions using words taken directly from the passage. You must write your answers in the answer booklet, not choose from multiple options. The instructions will specify a word limit (usually 1, 2, or 3 words, and/or a number).
typicalInstructions: Answer the questions using NO MORE THAN THREE WORDS from the passage.
Answer using NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER.
subsections.criticalRule: You must copy words exactly as they appear in the passage. You cannot change the form, add words, or paraphrase.

subsections.title: 1.2 What This Question Type Tests
subsections.description: Short Answer Questions assess several critical reading skills:

skills.meaning: Quickly locating specific information in the passage.
Selecting the exact words that answer the question.
Knowing what type of information is needed (Who? What? When? Where? Why? How?).
Adhering strictly to word limits.
Ensuring your answer makes grammatical sense with the question.
Understanding specific facts, not general ideas.

subsections.keyInsight: This is one of the most straightforward IELTS question types IF you follow the rules. Most mistakes come from exceeding word limits or changing the passage words.

rules.description: You must use the exact words from the passage. Do not: change singular to plural (or vice versa), change verb tenses, add articles (a, an, the) unless they're in the passage, paraphrase or use synonyms

example.passage: The research was funded by the European Space Agency.
example.question: Who funded the research?
example.correct: European Space Agency

rules.description: If the limit is 'NO MORE THAN THREE WORDS,' you can write: 1 word, 2 words, or 3 words. But NOT 4 or more words.

example.passage: The experiment took place in a secure underground laboratory.
example.question: Where did the experiment occur?
example.correct: underground laboratory (2 words)
example.wrong: secure underground laboratory (3 words - exceeds limit)

rules.rule: Rule 3: Hyphenated Words Count as One Word

rules.description: When instructions say 'AND/OR A NUMBER,' you can include numbers.
Your answer must make grammatical sense when combined with the question.

example.question: What did researchers discover?
example.passage: Researchers discovered that bees can recognize human faces.
example.correct: bees can recognize (or: recognize human faces)
example.wrong: that bees (grammatically incomplete)

types.description: These ask for specific concrete information.
examples: What type of energy does the plant use?
Where did the study take place?

types.description: These ask about methods, processes, or ways something is done.
examples: How did researchers collect the data?

types.description: These ask for causes, reasons, or purposes.
These ask for numbers, amounts, or durations.
examples: How long did the experiment last?

sections.title: SECTION 3: THE KEY DISTINCTION вЂ” DIRECT vs. INDIRECT ANSWERS

subsections.title: 3.1 Direct Answer Locations
subsections.description: Most short answer questions have direct answersвЂ”the information appears in a clear, straightforward sentence.

example.passage: The conference will be held in Singapore in October 2024.
example.question: Where will the conference take place?

subsections.title: 3.2 Indirect Answer Locations
subsections.description: Sometimes the answer is indirectвЂ”you must understand the context or find the information in a less obvious location.

example.passage: Originally scheduled for March, the launch was postponed until June due to technical issues.
example.question: When did the launch actually occur?
example.note: Indirect - you must understand 'postponed until' means the actual date

subsections.title: 3.3 Comparison: Direct vs. Indirect
subsections.description: Understanding the difference between direct and indirect answer locations:

comparisonTable.direct: The answer immediately follows the question keyword
comparisonTable.indirect: You must read surrounding sentences for context
Initially budgeted at $1 million, expenses eventually reached $2 million.

steps.title: Read the Instructions
actions: Note if numbers are allowed (AND/OR A NUMBER)
Never skip this stepвЂ”different questions may have different limits

steps.title: Read the Question Carefully
actions: Identify the question word: Who? What? When? Where? Why? How?
Determine what type of information you need (person, place, time, number, reason)

steps.title: Predict the Answer Type

predictions: Who? в†’ Look for a name or job title
When? в†’ Look for a date or time expression
Where? в†’ Look for a location
How many? в†’ Look for a number

actions: Scan for the keywords you underlined
Look for synonyms/paraphrases of those keywords

steps.title: Read Around the Answer

Read the complete sentence (and the sentence before/after if needed)

Is it a complete answer to what was asked?

subsections.title: 4.2 Time Management
subsections.rationale: You don't need to read the whole passage. You scan for specific information and extract it. This is one of the quickest question types if done correctly.

subsections.description: Understanding Question Words:

questionWords.example: Who conducted the study? в†’ 'Dr. Smith'
Where did it occur? в†’ 'Pacific Ocean'

questionWords.example: Why did prices rise? в†’ 'increased demand'

subsections.title: Amazon Rainforest Example
subsections.passage: The Amazon rainforest, often referred to as the 'lungs of the Earth,' covers approximately 5.5 million square kilometers across nine countries in South America. The forest is home to an estimated 390 billion individual trees representing over 16,000 species. Deforestation has been a growing concern, with approximately 17% of the forest lost over the past 50 years, primarily due to agricultural expansion and logging. Conservation efforts, led by organizations such as the World Wildlife Fund, have focused on establishing protected areas and promoting sustainable land use practices.

Scan: Find 'Amazon rainforest' in the passage
Locate: 'covers approximately 5.5 million square kilometers across nine countries'

Locate: 'primarily due to agricultural expansion and logging'
Note: 'logging' is also mentioned, but 'primarily due to' suggests agricultural expansion is the main cause

Check grammar: 'Which organization? World Wildlife Fund.' вњ“

subsections.title: The 10 Most Common Errors Students Make

mistakes.title: Mistake 1: Exceeding the Word Limit
mistakes.trap: You find the perfect answer, but it's 4 words and the limit is 3.

example.passage: The device was invented by renowned physicist Dr. Albert Chen.
example.question: Who invented the device?
example.wrong: Dr. Albert Chen (3 words - exceeds limit)
example.correct: Albert Chen (2 words) or if that doesn't make sense contextually: Dr. Chen (2 words)

mistakes.rule: When the perfect answer exceeds the limit, reduce to the essential information. Remove titles (Dr., Professor), articles (a, an, the), or adjectives if possible.

mistakes.title: Mistake 2: Changing the Words from the Passage
mistakes.trap: You paraphrase or use synonyms instead of copying exactly.

example.passage: The study was conducted over a twelve-month period.
example.question: How long did the study last?
example.correct: twelve-month period (exactly as written) or: twelve months

mistakes.rule: Copy words EXACTLY. Don't convert numbers between words and digits unless both forms appear in the passage.

mistakes.title: Mistake 3: Adding Extra Words
mistakes.trap: You add articles (a, an, the) or other words that aren't in the passage.

example.passage: The materials were transported by rail.
example.question: How were materials transported?
wrong: by rail (adding 'by' - not asked for, and 'rail' alone answers the question)
example.correct: rail

mistakes.rule: Use the minimum words necessary. If the question is 'How?' and the passage says 'by rail,' your answer is just 'rail' (unless the question specifically asks 'how were they transported' in which case 'by rail' might be needed for grammar).

mistakes.title: Mistake 4: Ignoring Grammar
mistakes.trap: Your answer doesn't make grammatical sense with the question.

example.passage: Researchers analyzed data from 500 participants.
example.question: What did researchers do?
example.wrong: data (grammatically incomplete: 'What did researchers do? Data.' makes no sense)
example.correct: analyzed data (grammatically complete: 'What did researchers do? Analyzed data.')

mistakes.rule: Always read your answer WITH the question. It must form a grammatically correct sentence or phrase.

mistakes.title: Mistake 5: Copying Surrounding Words
mistakes.trap: You copy words that are near the answer but don't actually answer the question.

example.passage: Due to severe weather conditions, the flight was delayed for three hours.
example.question: Why was the flight delayed?
wrong: the flight was (these words are in the sentence but don't answer WHY)
example.correct: severe weather conditions (this is the reason - follows 'due to')

mistakes.rule: Understand the question type. For 'Why?' questions, look for cause/reason signal words (because, due to, as a result of).

mistakes.title: Mistake 6: Misspelling or Changing Capitalization
mistakes.trap: You misspell the word or change capital letters.

example.passage: The conference took place in Copenhagen.
example.question: Where was the conference held?
example.correct: Copenhagen (exactly as written)

mistakes.rule: Copy spelling and capitalization EXACTLY. If it's capitalized in the passage, capitalize it in your answer.

mistakes.title: Mistake 7: Not Reading the Full Context
mistakes.trap: You grab the first word that matches a keyword without reading the complete sentence.

example.passage: While some experts recommend daily exercise, Dr. Martinez suggests that three times per week is sufficient for most people.
example.question: Who believes exercising three times weekly is enough?
example.wrong: some experts (you saw 'experts recommend' and stopped reading)
example.correct: Dr. Martinez (the sentence structure shows Dr. Martinez is the one with this specific opinion)

mistakes.rule: Always read the complete sentence and understand the context. Don't grab the first noun you see.

mistakes.title: Mistake 8: Including Question Words in Your Answer
mistakes.trap: You include words from the question in your answer unnecessarily.

example.passage: The population increased by 15% over the decade.
example.question: By how much did the population increase?
wrong: increased by 15% (repeating question words + exceeding word limit)

mistakes.rule: Your answer should only contain the NEW information requested, not repeat the question words.

mistakes.title: Mistake 9: Confusing Hyphenated Words and Word Count
mistakes.trap: You miscalculate how many words a hyphenated term counts as.

example.passage: The system uses state-of-the-art technology.
example.question: What type of technology is used?
example.wrong: state of the art technology (5 words - way over limit, and hyphens removed)
example.correct: state-of-the-art technology (2 words: 'state-of-the-art' = 1 hyphenated word, 'technology' = 1 word)

mistakes.rule: Hyphenated words = ONE word. Don't remove hyphens.

mistakes.title: Mistake 10: Leaving the Answer Blank
mistakes.trap: You can't find the answer, so you leave it blank.
mistakes.correct: Always write something. If you're unsure: Make your best guess using words from the relevant section, Ensure you stay within the word limit, Ensure it makes grammatical sense
mistakes.why: Blank = 0 marks. A guess = possible mark. IELTS doesn't deduct points for wrong answers.
mistakes.rule: Never leave any answer blank. Scan the passage for keywords and make an educated guess.
